package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed via phishing, not a package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: These malware families are remote access trojans (RATs) distributed via phishing campaigns using fake video conference invitations. They provide attackers with unauthorized remote access, credential theft, surveillance (including keylogging, audio/video capture), and system control capabilities, violating user privacy, data confidentiality, and system integrity.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (user opens malicious attachment or link)
execution_context.file_location: malicious executable delivered via phishing email (e.g., Win32.Backdoor.DCRat, Win32.Backdoor.NjRat)

malicious_snippets.code_language: powershell/c# (representative, as actual code is not shown)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code silently creates or modifies a registry key in HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run to add an entry named 'Updater' pointing to the RAT binary, ensuring the malware executes automatically at user logon, thereby establishing persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code modifies the Windows autorun registry key without user notification, a common persistence technique used by malware to maintain access after system reboot.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not silently add itself to autorun or modify registry run keys without explicit user consent and clear notification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate updaters or system utilities may register themselves for autorun, but typically do so with user awareness, clear branding, and visible installation prompts.
key_indicators: Creation of autorun entries with generic or misleading names like 'Updater'
No user-facing prompt or consent for autorun registration

malicious_snippets.code_language: c# / vb.net / python / java (depending on RAT variant)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code establishes an encrypted outbound connection to an attacker-controlled command-and-control server over port 443, collects system information, credentials, and screenshots, and exfiltrates this data to the remote server, enabling remote access and data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code initiates unsolicited outbound connections to external infrastructure and transmits sensitive data in encrypted form, which is a hallmark of RAT and data exfiltration activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not collect and transmit sensitive user data (such as credentials or screenshots) to unknown servers without user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote support tools may connect to known, trusted servers and transfer diagnostic data, but only with user consent, clear UI indicators, and to official domains.
key_indicators: Outbound connections to suspicious or non-standard domains
Encrypted exfiltration of sensitive data (system info, credentials, screenshots)
No user notification or legitimate reason for data transfer

malicious_snippets.code_language: c# / vb.net / java (depending on RAT variant)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code activates keylogging, clipboard capture, audio recording, and video capture modules in the background, collects user input and surveillance data, and prepares it for exfiltration to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code surreptitiously enables surveillance features (keylogging, audio/video recording, clipboard capture) without user knowledge, which is a core behavior of RATs and spyware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications do not record keystrokes, audio, or video, or capture clipboard data without explicit user permission and visible UI indicators.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Screen sharing or conferencing tools may access these features, but only with user consent, clear UI prompts, and visible indicators (e.g., recording icons).
key_indicators: Background activation of surveillance modules (keylogger, audio/video/clipboard capture)
No user notification or consent for surveillance activity
Data collection modules running persistently after installation

execution_context.trigger: runtime (on Android device, after user installs malicious APK)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: requestPermissions([READ_CONTACTS, READ_SMS, RECORD_AUDIO, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, CAMERA]); exfiltrate(contacts + sms + audio + location + video);
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code requests a broad set of sensitive permissions (contacts, SMS, audio, location, camera), collects the corresponding user data, and exfiltrates it to an attacker-controlled server, enabling full device surveillance and data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code requests excessive permissions unrelated to any legitimate app function and exfiltrates sensitive user data (contacts, SMS, audio, location, video) to an external server, which is typical of mobile RATs.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate apps should only request permissions necessary for their stated function and should never exfiltrate user data to unknown servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Messaging or conferencing apps may request some of these permissions, but not all at once, and only for legitimate, user-initiated features with clear consent and privacy disclosures.
key_indicators: Bulk permission requests at install or runtime
Exfiltration of sensitive data (contacts, SMS, audio, location, video) to unknown servers
No legitimate app functionality justifying requested permissions

attack_chain.action: User receives phishing email with fake video conference invitation (Skype, Zoom, Google Meets).
attack_chain.leads_to: User clicks malicious link or downloads attachment.

attack_chain.action: User downloads and executes malicious file (Windows executable or Android APK).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware installs and executes on victim system.

attack_chain.action: Malware establishes persistence via registry modification or autostart mechanisms.
Malware collects system information, credentials, and user data (keylogging, screenshots, audio/video capture).
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data is staged for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Malware exfiltrates collected data to attacker-controlled command-and-control servers over encrypted channels.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to victim data and remote control.

behavioral_signatures: Registry Run key or Startup folder modification for persistence by unknown executables
Unsolicited outbound network connections to suspicious or non-standard domains, especially those mimicking video conference services
Background activation of keylogging, clipboard, audio, or video capture modules without user notification
Bulk or excessive permission requests on Android apps not matching the app's stated purpose
Encrypted exfiltration of system or user data to external servers
file_indicators: APK files requesting excessive permissions (READ_CONTACTS, READ_SMS, RECORD_AUDIO, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, CAMERA)
Executables masquerading as video conference tools (e.g., filenames or icons mimicking Skype, Zoom, Google Meets)
network_indicators: Connections to attacker-controlled domains/IPs (often using domain names resembling legitimate video conference services but not matching official domains)
Use of non-standard ports or encrypted channels (e.g., custom TLS over port 443) for command-and-control communication
Frequent or persistent outbound traffic to unknown infrastructure after initial infection
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for registry or startup folder modifications by unknown executables, detect and alert on suspicious outbound network connections (especially to domains resembling video conference services but not matching official domains), flag executables or APKs requesting excessive or unrelated permissions, and alert on background activation of surveillance features (keylogging, audio/video capture) without user consent. Use threat intelligence feeds to block known RAT file hashes and C2 domains. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators for high-confidence detection.
